gaps.sentence: Only ___ people attended the talk, which was disappointing.
gaps.hint: countable plural; 'only a few' is the natural pattern
gaps.explanation: 'Only a few people' is the standard way to say a small number; 'only few' is not used.

gaps.sentence: There are too ___ tourists in Venice in August.
gaps.explanation: 'Too many' is used before countable plurals like tourists; 'too much' is for uncountables.

gaps.sentence: ___ everyone in the office passed the safety test.
gaps.hint: the only adverb that can modify 'everyone'
gaps.explanation: 'Almost everyone' is the standard pattern; 'each', 'all' and 'every' cannot directly precede 'everyone'.

gaps.sentence: I don't like this colour — do you have it in ___ colours?
gaps.explanation: 'Other colours' uses 'other' as an adjective before the plural noun; 'another' is followed by singular nouns.

gaps.sentence: She carried a suitcase in ___ hand.
gaps.explanation: 'Each hand' views the two hands individually; 'every hand' is not used for body parts this way.

gaps.sentence: Don't worry, we still have ___ time before the gates close.
gaps.hint: positive meaning: there is some time; 'time' is uncountable
gaps.explanation: 'A little time' means some time, which reassures; 'time' is uncountable.

gaps.hint: general statement without 'the' — 'people' has no article
gaps.explanation: 'Most people' means people in general; 'most of' needs 'the' (most of the people).

gaps.sentence: ___ of my two brothers work in banking.
gaps.explanation: 'Both of my two brothers work ...' is correct; 'all' and 'none' are not used for two.
